{"id": "2:266/q29", "question": "What happened in the report of Umar asking about the parable?", "turns_on": "The reports vary in Ibn Abbas's wording and whether Umar or Ibn Abbas states the late-life analogy.", "positions": [{"id": "2:266/q29/p1", "position": "Umar pressed the Companions for an answer, Ibn Abbas interpreted deeds ruined after obedience by Satan-led sins, and Umar approved.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi describe Umar's anger when they deferred instead of saying whether they knew; Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Kashshaf, Ibn Kathir, al-Biqai, al-Durr, al-Alusi and Ibn Ashur transmit the wealthy worshipper explanation. Al-Qurtubi calls it an established Bukhari report, Ibn Kathir says al-Bukhari alone transmits this interpretation, al-Biqai specifies Bukhari's tafsir, and al-Alusi also names al-Hakim and Ibn Jarir. Al-Durr adds that Ibn Abbas first whispered his thought. Baghawi transmits a version through Ubayd ibn Umayr in which Ibn Abbas says show-off and Umar gives the wealthy worshipper analogy. Al-Itqan explicitly locates the exchange in Bukhari; the Bukhari report itself has Umar ask, Ibn Abbas explain the wealthy obedient man's Satan-led sins consuming his deeds, and Umar accept it."}, {"id": "2:266/q29/p2", "position": "Another telling has Ibn Abbas say a person ends a long good life with evil when deeds are most needed, and Umar accepts or marvels.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari and Ibn Atiyya transmit this formulation. Ibn Abi Mulayka attributes the late-life summary to Umar in Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi. Al-Durr gives several versions, including an evil final deed and persistent late sin; al-Alusi reports Ata's version."}]}
{"id": "2:266/q30", "question": "What other transmitted reports are brought to bear on this verse?", "turns_on": "These are separate reports used as illustrations, not rival accounts of one event.", "positions": [{"id": "2:266/q30/p1", "position": "The Prophet prayed for his broadest provision in old age near life's end.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir attributes the report to al-Hakim; al-Durr transmits it from Aisha."}, {"id": "2:266/q30/p2", "position": "A Prophetic report associates intense heat with Hell's breath and the Fire's complaint.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya cites it to illuminate the wind's heat; al-Qurtubi adds delaying prayer in severe heat."}, {"id": "2:266/q30/p3", "position": "Ikrima says every worldly kind of tree exists in Paradise, even colocynth.", "reasons": "Ibn Abi Hatim transmits the statement beside the garden's fruits."}, {"id": "2:266/q30/p4", "position": "Ibn Abbas also describes a man who wastes his garden in youth and loses it in old age, when weak children cannot help restore or support him.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir preserves this as an alternate Ibn Abbas report."}, {"id": "2:266/q30/p5", "position": "Ali asked forgiveness for devotions whose intention his heart later contradicted.", "reasons": "Al-Qashani uses the prayer to illustrate later inner corruption of good action."}, {"id": "2:266/q30/p6", "position": "The Prophet advised Muadh to make religion sincere so even little work suffices.", "reasons": "Bursavi cites the instruction given when Muadh was sent to Yemen."}, {"id": "2:266/q30/p7", "position": "A Prophetic counsel surveys prayer, faith, fasting, jihad, charity, Ayat al-Kursi, prophets and scriptures, and practical piety.", "reasons": "Ibn Hibban reports the Prophet praising the mosque greeting and prayer whether plentiful or sparse; faith, good character, safety from harm, long prayer and abstaining from sins; obligatory fasting and its reward; costly jihad; and a poor person's strenuous gift. The report calls Ayat al-Kursi the greatest revelation, compares the heavens and Throne to a ring and desert, counts prophets, messengers and revealed books, and conveys teachings attributed to Abraham's and Moses' scrolls on justice, reflection and accountability. It also counsels taqwa, Qur'an, remembrance, restrained speech, companionship with the poor, gratitude, truthfulness, planning and self-correction."}]}
{"id": "2:266/q31", "question": "What inward process can destroy a deed or spiritual progress?", "turns_on": "Whether the inner ruin is corruption of a deed's intention or reversal of a seeker's ascent.", "positions": [{"id": "2:266/q31/p1", "position": "Ego, self-regard or ostentation turns a good deed's inner motions into Satan's whirlwind, and its fire consumes the deed.", "reasons": "Al-Qashani includes charity done for God's pleasure before the ego reappears; he cites Ali's prayer about intentions later contradicted by the heart."}, {"id": "2:266/q31/p2", "position": "A seeker rises toward the divine unseen realm, turns back to worldly illusion, and loses the effort.", "reasons": "Al-Baydawi likens the scattered effort to dust; Bursavi gives the same spiritual parallel."}]}
{"id": "2:266/q32", "question": "How should a giver protect work from the ruin pictured here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:266/q32/p1", "position": "Keep sincerity at the root of worship and resist ostentation before and during action.", "reasons": "Bursavi quotes Qushayri's contrast of sincere and hypocritical spending, flourishing crops and ruined bargains. Bursavi says fruits depend on roots, names love of the world and immediate pleasure as chief causes, and counsels examining the heart before worship, removing showy thoughts and resisting them. He distinguishes expecting notice, desiring praise and status, then accepting that desire. Al-Tabatabai adds love of wealth and status, pride, conceit and miserliness, saying reflection exposes their harm. Jishumi reports the exhortation to preserve charity by avoiding acts that invalidate it."}, {"id": "2:266/q32/p2", "position": "Preserve acts of worship from whatever would spoil them, as the aged owner's needed garden is destroyed.", "reasons": "Jishumi draws this general requirement from the garden's destruction when the owner and weak children need it most; he also reports the charity-specific injunction against invalidating one's gift."}, {"id": "2:266/q32/p3", "position": "Have a share in every kind of good deed, hoping some of it will bring deliverance in the afterlife.", "reasons": "Ibn Hibban's heading recommends breadth in good deeds for hope of deliverance in the afterlife."}]}
{"id": "2:266/q33", "question": "How is the wider spending passage organized?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:266/q33/p1", "position": "It forms a connected teaching on the purpose, manner, quality, recipient and reward of giving.", "reasons": "Al-Tabatabai says the connected themes suggest revelation as one unit: seven-hundredfold or greater growth, sincere fruitfulness, loss through ostentation or harm, giving good wealth, aid to the needy detained in God's path, and great reward. He orders these as giving for God, without reproach or injury, from good property, to the needy, for reward."}]}
{"id": "2:266/q34", "question": "How does the extended garden image give the warning force?", "turns_on": "Whether the source emphasizes the scene's accumulated particulars or general principles of figurative assertion.", "positions": [{"id": "2:266/q34/p1", "position": "Its accumulated details complete the illustrative comparison and make the loss feel inescapably severe.", "reasons": "Al-Itqan calls the sequence from crops and rivers through aged owner, weak offspring, fiery storm and burning exhaustive elaboration, eliminating imagined escapes; it reports Ibn Abi al-Isba's distinction between completion, supplementation and exhaustive elaboration. Ibn Ashur calls the scene an extended illustrative simile that magnifies the loss."}, {"id": "2:266/q34/p2", "position": "A figure gains persuasive force through a shared quality and through an asserted meaning supported by an observable sign.", "reasons": "In general discussions of figuration, Jurjani compares sewing with chainmail making, faces with suns and brave men with lions to distinguish shared qualities from surface labels; his courage example distinguishes a quality from every outward act. He says figures depend on interpreted meaning, whereas plain glosses lose their force; representational merit lies in how a quality is asserted, and kinaya argues from a sign. His lion example contrasts certain, inherent courage with mere possibility."}]}

{"id": "2:266/q36", "question": "What background does al-Alusi give about composing the commentary cited for this verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:266/q36/p1", "position": "He developed exegetical insights early, drew on predecessors, began writing after a vision in 1252 AH, and reports the work's naming and patronage.", "reasons": "In his preface al-Alusi recalls exegetical work before twenty, use of earlier scholars and delays in writing; he dates a Friday-night vision to Rajab 1252 AH, interpreted its command to mend heaven and earth as a prompt to write, began on 16 Shaban, and says Ali Rida Pasha named Ruh al-maani under Sultan Mahmud Khan al-Adli."}]}

{"id": "2:27/q02", "question": "How is ٱلَّذِينَ parsed?", "turns_on": "Attachment to the preceding fāsiqīn or a separate condemnatory sentence.", "positions": [{"id": "2:27/q02/p1", "position": "It is accusative as an adjective of the preceding fāsiqīn.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan and Ibn Ashur prefer syntactic continuity; Baydawi says the description confirms their transgression."}, {"id": "2:27/q02/p2", "position": "It is a new subject whose predicate is 'those are the losers'.", "reasons": "Alusi calls this almost parenthetical; al-Samin gives the resulting final-clause parse."}, {"id": "2:27/q02/p3", "position": "It is detached for censure or predicate of an omitted pronoun.", "reasons": "Nahhas and Qurtubi supply huwa/hum; Abu Hayyan also allows accusative censure."}]}
{"id": "2:27/q03", "question": "What does 'breaking' mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:27/q03/p1", "position": "Undoing a firmly secured bond, then abandoning or opposing its terms.", "reasons": "The sources compare untying rope and dismantling a building. {"id": "2:27/q04", "question": "Why describe breach as untying?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:27/q04/p1", "position": "The covenant is an imagined cord binding two parties; breach loosens its strands.", "reasons": "Baydawi and Bursevi explain the image. {"id": "2:27/q05", "question": "What can ʿahd mean in Arabic?", "turns_on": "The word has several attested senses; the verse's referent is a separate question.", "positions": [{"id": "2:27/q05/p1", "position": "A charge, instruction, testament, or entrusted duty.", "reasons": "Ibn Jawzi and Ibn Faris cite the charge in 36:60 and revelation to Abraham and Ishmael in 2:125; some group revelation with instruction."}, {"id": "2:27/q05/p2", "position": "A binding pact, security guarantee, oath, or agreement.", "reasons": "Ibn Faris gives binding security; 9:4 illustrates treaty protection, while Ibn Qutayba reads 16:91 as oath and another reading calls it agreement."}, {"id": "2:27/q05/p3", "position": "In other uses it means keeping faith, safeguarding, monotheism, revelation, or prophethood.", "reasons": "Ibn Jawzi cites 7:102, 19:87, 2:125, and 2:124; a prophetic saying makes faithful keeping part of faith."}, {"id": "2:27/q05/p4", "position": "Related forms name a period, first rain, refuge, covenanting person, sale document, unresolved matter, or renewed care.", "reasons": "Ibn Faris catalogs the uses; Ibn Jawzi distinguishes one-sided taʿahhad from reciprocal taʿāhad."}]}
{"id": "2:27/q06", "question": "Which covenant is broken here?", "turns_on": "The rival grounds are transmitted obligations, rational proof, primordial testimony, or a specific historical pledge.", "positions": [{"id": "2:27/q06/p1", "position": "God's general commands and prohibitions transmitted in revelation and through messengers.", "reasons": "Breaking means not acting on them. {"id": "2:282/q01", "question": "How is the opening address construed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:282/q01/p1", "position": "The address calls believers through the standard ya ayyuhā construction.", "reasons": "SIBAWAYH (author): A waṣl alif drops after preceding speech because earlier words remove the need for an onset; Sībawayh compares this to dropping hāʾ in vocative speech. SIBAWAYH (author): An annexed noun used as a vocative is accusative by an unspoken verb; the singular vocative is nominative in form but occupies an accusative position. SIBAWAYH (author): An annexed adjective of a vocative should be accusative whenever the corresponding singular adjective is accusative. SIBAWAYH (أبو عمرو): Yūnus reports that Abū ʿAmr and the people of Medina say ya akhānā Zayd, treating the adjective like a standalone vocative. SIBAWAYH (author): Ya akhānā Zaydan is more common because speakers restore the original accusative after the name leaves the vocative position. SIBAWAYH (author): A standalone singular vocative is raised without tanwīn because frequent use led speakers to shorten it and treat it like an interjection. SIBAWAYH (رؤبة): Ruʾbah's verse ya Naṣru Naṣran Naṣran supports the accusative appositional repetition; Abū ʿAmr's form restarts the vocative. SIBAWAYH (author): The adjective of a standalone vocative differs from that of amsi because nominative marking is consistent across vocatives. SIBAWAYH (الخليل): Al-Khalīl says annexed vocatives and long indefinite calls such as ya rajulan ṣāliḥan are accusative. SIBAWAYH (author

): Coordination such as ya Zayd wa-ʿAmr shares the vocative particle across names; the second name is not an adjective. SIBAWAYH (author): A standalone singular vocative is raised like qablu and baʿdu, though it occupies an accusative position. SIBAWAYH (الخليل): Al-Khalīl also allows the adjective to be nominative as an adjective of the raised vocative. {"id": "2:282/q02", "question": "What transaction brought the verse down?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:282/q02/p1", "position": "The reported occasion is the forward sale called salam.", "reasons": "TAB-FULL (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas says the verse was revealed specifically about forward purchase of wheat by known measure and due date. JISHUMI (ابن عباس): Ibn ʿAbbās says the verse was revealed specifically about salam sales. IBNATIYYA-FULL (ابن عباس): Ibn ʿAbbās says the debt-documentation verse was revealed specifically concerning forward sales (salam); Ibn ʿAṭiyya says such sales in Medina occasioned it, but the rule covers all debts by consensus. IBNATIYYA-FULL (قتادة والربيع وغيرهما): They read the summons as one to give initial testimony. The verse was revealed when a claimant sought witnesses among many people, who hesitated to come forward. TABRISI (ابن عباس): Ibn ʿAbbās says the verse was revealed specifically concerning forward sale and testifies that God permitted a guaranteed sale to a known term. IBNJAWZI-ZAD (ابن عباس): Ibn ʿAbbas says the verse was revealed specifically about salam, an advance-purchase transaction. RAZI-FULL (ابن عباس): Ibn ʿAbbas says the verse was revealed about forward sales: people in Medina prepaid for dates two or three years ahead, and the Prophet required known measure, weight, and term. QURTUBI-FULL (ابن عباس): He says the verse was revealed specifically about salam, prompted by the people of Medina, but by consensus it covers all deferred debt transactions. NASAFI-FULL (ابن عباس): Ibn ʿAbbās says this concerns salam; after forbidding usury, God permitted a guaranteed advance sale for a known term and revealed the longest verse, requiring a term for salam. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (ابن عباس): Ibn ʿAbbās says the debt-document verse was revealed specifically about forward-sale transactions in Medina; consensus extends it to all debts. IBNKATHIR-FULL (ابن عباس): Through Mujahid, Ibn Abbas says the verse was revealed concerning salam, an advance payment due at a known term. DURR-FULL (ابن عباس): The verse was revealed concerning advance purchase of grain in a known measure for a known term. DURR-FULL (النبي): When people in Medina prepaid for fruit for two or three years, the Prophet required a known measure, weight, and term. ELMALILI (author): One report gives the occasion of revelation as salam, paying in advance for goods delivered later, though the ruling covers every kind of sale and debt transaction. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR (İbn Abbas): Ibn Abbas says the verse was revealed about salam, a sale paid for in advance with goods delivered later, for example at harvest."}]}
{"id": "2:282/q03", "question": "How does the verse follow the usury prohibition?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:282/q03/p1", "position": "The debt rule follows the usury ban by permitting and safeguarding lawful credit.", "reasons": "SIBAWAYH (author): The tribal name Ḥayy ibn Bahdalah supplies evidence for ḥayawī and for vocalizing yāʾ before wāw. SIBAWAYH (author): A preceding fatḥa or ḍamma also prevents imāla, as in ribāb, jimād, and al-balbāl. SIBAWAYH (author): Plural patterns that already have broken plural forms can be broken again as names: examples include aʿdāl to aʿādīl and aqwāl to aqāwīl, alongside abyāt, anʿām, and ajriba. THALABI (ابن عباس): When God prohibited usury, He permitted deferred sale; tadayantum means you transact debt with one another, including loans, forward sales, and other deferred obligations. WAHIDI-BASIT (ابن عباس): Ibn ʿAbbās connects the verse with God forbidding usury while permitting salam, or advance purchase on credit. WAHIDI-WAJIZ (author): After prohibiting usury, God permits forward-credit sales and commands writing and witnessing deferred debts to protect property; the trust exception in 2:283 abrogates this command. | mentions 2:283 JISHUMI (author): After forbidding usury, God permits salam and debts; after commanding respite, he also commands fulfillment before documentation and witnesses. BAGHAWI-FULL (ابن عباس): After forbidding usury, God permitted salam, an advance purchase secured to a fixed term, in this verse. KASHSHAF-FULL (ابن عباس): Ibn ʿAbbās says the verse concerns salam: after usury was forbidden, advance sale for a guaranteed term was permitted and the longest verse revealed for it. RAZI-FULL (author): The detailed debt-recording rule follows commands to give charity, avoid usury, and remain mindful of God: preserving lawful wealth enables those duties and protects worldly and religious interests. | mentions 4:5 RAZI-FULL (قوم من المفسرين): Some exegetes take the debt transaction here as salam, which provides the benefits sought through usury by a lawful route; the author approves this as a second coherent link. RAZI-FULL (author): A second account of the passage’s arrangement says the ban on usury is followed by permission for salam, which offers the same desired benefits through lawful means. BAYDAWI-FULL (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas says the verse concerns advance sale, which God allowed when forbidding usury. NASAFI-FULL (ابن عباس): Ibn ʿAbbās says this concerns salam; after forbidding usury, God permitted a guaranteed advance sale for a known term and revealed the longest verse, requiring a term for salam. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): After commands to spend in God's path and leave usury, this verse offers a lawful way to grow wealth and gives detailed rules for protecting it. BURHAN (أبو عبيد القاسم بن سلام، أحمد بن يحيى ثعلب): One view takes the seven ahruf as seven Arab tribal dialects distributed across the Qur'an, not seven alternatives for each word; the dialects differ while meanings remain the same. BURHAN (ابن عبد البر): Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr argues seven tribal languages would not have prompted companions to condemn one another's readings; ʿUmar and Hisham were both Quraysh yet differed, and ʿUmar challenged Hisham. BIQAI-FULL (author): Charity and avoiding usury purify wealth while principal remains lawful and insolvent debtors receive respite; this may tempt debtors to feign insolvency, so the debt verse teaches preservation through documentation. DURR-FULL (ابن شهاب): Ibn Shihab says the last Qur'anic material with the Throne was the usury verse and the debt verse. ELMALILI (author): Any debt transaction with a specified, known due date should be written; credit trading remains permissible despite the ban on usury, provided the due date is known and documented. IBNASHUR-FULL (جماعة منهم أبو بكر الباقلائي وابن عبد البر وأبو بكر بن العربي والطبري والطحاوي): Al-Baqillani, Ibn Abd al-Barr, Ibn al-Arabi, al-Tabari, and al-Tahawi, with this view attributed to Ibn Uyayna and Ibn Wahb, hold that the seven-letter license was later abrogated after allowing tribal dialects. IBNASHUR-FULL (أبو علي الاهوازي وابن عبد البر وابن قتيبة): Abu Ali al-Ahwazi, Ibn Abd al-Barr, and Ibn Qutayba restrict the seven dialects to Mudar tribes: Quraysh, Hudhayl, Kinana, Qays, Dabba, Taym al-Ribab, and Asad ibn Khuzayma. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): Ibn Ashur says Uthman’s phrase may mean Quraysh speech predominated in the Quran, or that its dialect absorbed tribal forms through Mecca’s centrality and the Ukaz market. IBNASHUR-FULL (أبو عبيدة وابن عطية وأبو حاتم والباقلاني): Abu Ubayda, Ibn Atiyya, Abu Hatim, and al-Baqillani identify the seven dialects as Quraysh, Hudhayl, Taym al-Ribab, Azd, Rabi'a, Hawazin, and Sa'd ibn Bakr. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): In pre-Islamic and early Islamic practice a guardian could be a senior relative, father, trustee, or tribal notable; the Prophet told Hawāzin’s delegation to bring their ʿurafāʾ to present their case. IBNASHUR-FULL (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): In the Hawāzin delegation report, the Prophet directs them to bring their tribal representatives to him, illustrating the early role of ʿurafāʾ in tribal affairs. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR (author): Because ordinary borrowing is necessary and abuse led to usury, the Qur'an permits loans and other lawful deferred contracts after forbidding interest; writing, witnesses, collateral, and trust help ensure timely full repayment and prevent forgetting or denial."}]}
{"id": "2:282/q04", "question": "Which debts and transactions does تداينتم include?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:282/q04/p1", "position": "The wording covers deferred obligations, including sales and loans where applicable.", "reasons": "TAB-FULL (author): Tadayantum covers deferred sales and purchases, lending, and other debt exchanges due at a known, fixed time; it includes loans, forward sales, and permissible sales with deferred payment. IBNATIYYA-FULL (ابن عباس): Ibn ʿAbbās says the debt-documentation verse was revealed specifically concerning forward sales (salam); Ibn ʿAṭiyya says such sales in Medina occasioned it, but the rule covers all debts by consensus. udes every deferred debt, which commentators and jurists accept.
